definition: Difficult to control, manage, or solve.
example: The team confronted an intractable software defect.
nuance: Intractable can describe people, conditions, or problems.
options: The intractable dispute resisted every proposed compromise.
The intractable dispute was easily settled in seconds.
The problem was intractable because everyone readily agreed.
Intractable meant the dispute had never begun.
reasons: Resistance to resolution illustrates an intractable problem.
Ready agreement does not illustrate resistance.

practice.prompt: A city has tried for years to stop one low-lying neighborhood from flooding.
options: The engineer said the flooding was intractable, meaning it stayed within one tract of land.
Despite new drains and pumps, the intractable flooding returned every spring.
Residents called the flooding intractable after one sandbag stopped it for good.
Because the floodwater was intractable, nobody could see or touch it.
reasons: The word has nothing to do with tracts of land; it describes a problem that will not yield.
A problem that keeps coming back after repeated fixes is stubbornly resisting a solution.
A problem ended by a single easy step is the opposite of one that defies solving.
This confuses the word with intangible; it is about resisting control, not being invisible.
